deep.reconstruction:
The page has four separate notes. They are dated by context to after Möbius's 'Der barycentrische Calcul' (1827); the pentagon note fits Gauss's pentagon studies (1823 onward).

(1) RESULTANT CALCULUS. In Möbius's barycentric calculus a point P carrying mass m is a formal object mP. Gauss proposes a dual 'Resultantencalcul' whose objects are lines carrying forces, each acting along the line in a definite sense. If a, b, c, d, ... are such lines with force magnitudes proportional to α, β, γ, δ, ..., then αa + βb + γc + δd + ... = 0 is to mean that the forces are in equilibrium.

Modern form (my filling): in the plane, a force F = (Fx, Fy) acting along a line through a point (x, y) is the triple (Fx, Fy, M) with M = x*Fy - y*Fx. This is a sliding vector and the triple does not depend on which point of the line is chosen. Lines with forces then form a 3-dimensional vector space, the same space as homogeneous line coordinates. So in the plane the resultant calculus is exactly the projective dual of the barycentric calculus (points with masses = homogeneous point vectors). Equilibrium means vanishing of both the resultant force and the resultant moment.

In space, forces along lines together with couples form a 6-dimensional space (wrenches; Plücker coordinates when restricted to single forces). This justifies Gauss's guess that it is 'vermuthlich noch umfassender' (presumably even more comprehensive).

(2) 'B - C = a i'. If B and C are points of the line a, the barycentric difference B - C (total mass 0) is the free vector along a. Gauss proposes to equate it with a times a factor i, presumably a scalar fixing the force magnitude. The precise modern counterpart is the combinatorial (Grassmann) product of the two points. Computed with (Bx, By, 1) and (Cx, Cy, 1), the cross product gives (By - Cy, Cx - Bx, Bx*Cy - By*Cx). This is, up to sign convention, the force C - B placed on the line BC, including its moment. This is my interpretation.

(3) PENTAGON. The question is what masses (applied barycentrically at the vertices) or forces (applied resultantly along the sides) should be put on a pentagon. The aim is that they and their equivalents on the inner pentagon, formed by the diagonals, stand in the simplest possible relations. The struck word, replaced by 'Winkelpunkte' (vertices), may be 'Seiten' or 'Ecken'. This is a research question only; no computation is given. The context is the pentagon investigations (Gauss's 1823 area formula; Möbius).

(4) COLLINEATION. Two systems of points (or of lines) are collinear (in modern terms, related by a projective collineation) if between any 5 points (lines) of one system and the 5 corresponding ones of the other the same linear equation can be set up. Reading (mine): each point carries a fixed homogeneous representative (a 'mass'), and every relation Σ α_k P_k = 0 among corresponding points is preserved. This holds exactly when the correspondence is induced by a linear map T on homogeneous coordinates, since Σ α_k P_k = 0 implies Σ α_k T P_k = 0. Five points are the generic number carrying exactly one relation in space, where homogeneous coordinates are 4-dimensional. In the plane, 4 would suffice and 5 points give a 2-parameter family of relations. The next page continues with an invariant characterisation via the ratio (PA·QB)/(PB·QA) of point-to-line distances.
errors: No computational errors; the page is programmatic.

'B - C = a i' conflates a free vector (B - C, a mass-zero barycentric object) with a line-bound force. It is consistent only if 'i' or the operation absorbs the positional (moment) information. The correct counterpart is the exterior/Grassmann product B∧C, not the difference.

In the planar case the number 5 in the collineation definition is more than needed: 4 points in general position already carry one linear relation. 5 is the right count for space. The condition also tacitly requires a consistent choice of weights (homogeneous representatives) for all points; otherwise the 'same equation' is ill-defined.

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in and reaction to Möbius's barycentric calculus is known. An explicit sketch of a dual 'resultant calculus' of force-carrying lines (Möbius's Statik 1837, Grassmann 1844) is a notable but programmatic unpublished detail with no worked theory. The collineation definition is essentially Möbius's viewpoint.
